items.descriptionOriginal: At 75, Abdul Majeed Zargar still works with a craft that few people outside Kashmir's weaving workshops know exists. From his home in Amda Kadal Jogiwan, Srinagar, he hand-carves the wooden shuttle used to weave the region's celebrated Pashmina shawls. Known locally as the Mukh, the small tool carries the thread that makes every woven piece possible. Zargar is believed to be the last craftsman in Kashmir who makes these shuttles by hand. For nearly five decades, he has shaped wood into a tool that connects generations of weavers, even as the traditional skills behind Kashmir's textile heritage face declining demand. His story began with uncertainty. Before finding his calling, Zargar tried his hand at silver-making and knife-making. Neither trade worked for him, and he eventually turned to making Mukhs. Learning the craft took almost a year, during which he struggled to produce pieces that met the standards of experienced weavers. When he finally had a few shuttles ready to sell, he carried them from one workshop to another. Most people turned him away. He was close to abandoning the craft when a meeting in Khayam changed his life. Three shuttles that changed everything Zargar approached a sazvari, a trader who bought and sold weaving tools. The trader invited him upstairs, where experienced craftsmen were working. Nervous, Zargar showed them his handmade Mukhs. Having once struggled to find buyers for his work, Zargar now makes wooden shuttles that weavers value for their quality and durability. Photograph: ( Facebook/The Better India) They examined the pieces carefully and pointed out their flaws. Yet, before he left, they bought three pairs. The shuttles were not good enough for weaving, but the craftsmen wanted to encourage him to continue. When Zargar returned months later, he found the pieces still hanging on the wall. They had never been used. He asked why they had bought them if they were faulty. Their answer stayed with him: "If we had not bought them, you would have lost hope." The craftsmen also recommended him to other weavers and traders, helping him find customers who needed new shuttles or repairs. Slowly, his work improved, and his Mukhs became known for their quality and durability. There were times when weavers had to wait months for one of his handmade tools . That early encouragement became the foundation of a career spanning five decades. The tiny tool behind every Pashmina A Mukh may appear insignificant beside a finished shawl, but it performs one of the most important tasks in traditional weaving. The shuttle carries the weft yarn back and forth across the warp threads on a loom, allowing the fabric to take shape. With few young people willing to learn the craft, Zargar is turning to the next generation in his own family to keep the skill alive. Photograph: ( Facebook/Kashmir Life ) Without it, the loom cannot function. Every handwoven Pashmina or Tusha shawl depends on this simple movement before it can reach the stages of dyeing, embroidery and finishing. Zargar calls the Mukh the basis of Pashmina . Its importance lies not in its size or appearance, but in the work it enables. The tool connects the weaver to the larger ecosystem of Kashmiri textile artisans, whose skills transform delicate fibres into intricate fabrics. Over the years, Zargar has also improved the traditional design. Earlier, the metal components of the shuttle were made of iron, which could rust. He replaced them with brass, making the tool more durable and resistant to corrosion. Today, factory-made shuttle boats are cheaper and more readily available. But Zargar believes that the handmade Mukhs remain superior in quality and longevity. His tools are carved entirely by hand using chisels and files, without modern machinery. Passing down a dying craft The challenge facing Zargar is not simply the availability of tools, but the shrinking demand for traditional handloom weaving itself. As power looms replace handlooms and younger people move towards other professions, the need for handmade shuttles has declined. For Zargar, making Mukhs is about more than earning a livelihood. It is about preserving a small but essential part of Kashmir's Pashmina-making tradition. Photograph: ( Facebook/Daily Excelsior ) Zargar has tried to teach others, but finding willing apprentices has been difficult. Many young people prefer computer-based jobs or work in cities, leaving fewer people interested in learning a specialised craft that requires patience and years of practice. Despite decades of recognition and support from the Department of Handicrafts, he worries that awards alone cannot preserve the skill. What matters, he said, is that the craft continues. He is now teaching his son, hoping the knowledge will survive beyond his own lifetime. The work remains painstaking, and the future uncertain, but Zargar continues to carve the wooden tools that weavers depend on. "I do not know what will happen after me," he told Kashmir Life. "But as long as I can hold my tools, I will keep making them." For Kashmir's Pashmina, the survival of a centuries-old weaving tradition may depend on a small wooden shuttle, and on whether someone is willing to learn how to make it. Sources ' Kashmir's Last Shuttle ': by Afreen Ashraf for Kashmir Life, Published on 10 July, 2026, ' Meet Abdul Majeed Zargar: Kashmir's Last Surviving 'Mukh ' Craftsman': by Jahangeer Ganaie for Kashmir News Observer, Published on 19 May, 2025 ' For Want of a Tool, Kashmir's Famed Pashmina Industry Is Crumbling ': for Moneycontrol, Published in 2021

items.title: Από 27 ραπτομηχανές έως εργασίες στο εργοστάσιο, πώς οι γυναίκες Warli του Aarey ράβουν νέες αρχές
items.titleOriginal: From 27 Sewing Machines to Factory Jobs, How Aarey’s Warli Women Are Stitching New Beginnings
items.description: Καθώς πηγαίνω στο δάσος Aarey της Βομβάης (ο τελευταίος πράσινος πνεύμονας της πόλης), παίρνω τον υπόγειο διάδρομο του μετρό Aqua Line. Αλλά καθ' όλη τη διάρκεια της διαδρομής μου, δεν μπορώ να αγνοήσω την ενοχλητική αίσθηση ότι αυτή η επιλογή μεταφοράς είναι σχεδόν ιεροσυλία, δεδομένου ότι η κατασκευή του προκάλεσε σάλο το 2019 όταν απείλησε να εκτοπίσει 27 κοινότητες Warli Adivasi.…
items.descriptionOriginal: While making my way to Mumbai's Aarey Forest (the city's last green lung), I take the Aqua Line underground metro corridor. But throughout my ride, I can't ignore the nagging feeling that this choice of transport is almost sacrilege, given that its construction sparked an uproar in 2019 when it threatened to displace 27 Warli Adivasi communities that have called the forest home since the 1950s. But the metro is what will get me to my destination in the quickest time, and so I ignore the nagging guilt. In 2019, many of my trips were to the same forest to document the protests (as a journalism student); today, the purpose of my trip is different. The years have witnessed the community women being empowered through a stitching programme that has "changed their lives", according to many of their accounts. What began as an informal way of channelling their skills into a purpose has now solidified into formal jobs in factories across Mumbai. Their stories echo the resilience of a community that has repeatedly had to adapt to a city growing around it. Their stories echo the resilience of a community that has repeatedly had to adapt to a city growing around it. The same women whose homes and livelihoods once stood at the centre of a battle over Aarey's future are now finding new ways to assert their place within Mumbai's economic landscape. Through sewing, they have transformed a skill passed down within the community into a source of income, confidence and independence. What began as a small stitching initiative has, for some, become a pathway to formal employment. A conversation among the trees It's a Sunday morning when I plan my visit to the forest. While I was told that the women who work through the week would be at home (Sunday is their weekly off from the factory), the hamlets seem quiet. Surekha Burkhud (40), who lives in Khambachapada and has stayed back, shares that the factory had a sudden urgent requirement for a bulk order, and so the women were called. But she is quick to add, "The women don't mind going because they are paid OT (overtime). This is double their usual day's pay." It's just Surekha and me and the trees for company: chickoo, guava, jamun and ber (Indian jujube) . Drawing on context from them, she starts by emphasising the community's love for the trees in Aarey. "These were planted by some of the oldest members. When the metro was being built, we were so disturbed by the fact that our trees would get destroyed. They are our life," she shares. According to reports, hours after the Bombay High Court (HC) dismissed several petitions of the locals seeking Aarey to be declared a protected area, on 4 October 2019, opposing the construction of a 33-hectare metro car-shed in the forest, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) felled approximately 2,700 trees over the course of two days. Several protestors were detained, beaten up, and 29 were arrested on serious charges under Section 353, Section 332, Section 143 and Section 149. Seeing it pained the community members. I ask Surekha whether she's travelled by metro, given their aversion to its construction. She admits she has. "I was scared of being underground for so long," she sheepishly acknowledges. While admittedly the Aqua Line 3 has eased public commute for Mumbai's residents — reports had pegged the metro to eventually carry around 1.7 million passengers every day and bring down the number of vehicles on the road by up to 650,000 — Surekha says they find it inconvenient to access the metro as the car shed is built close to the hamlets, but the actual boarding gate is near Seepz. A PARI report had documented the plight of other Warli Adivasi families that weren't as fortunate as hers. Locals estimate that 70 Adivasi families lost their homes to the metro project. From 27, the number of padas is now down to 15. In addition to this, a common complaint they have is that because of the car shed area, water collects during the rains, causing flooding. That being said, the community is happy that for "the time being" their hamlet is safe. "But we never know," Surekha shrugs. A PARI report had documented the plight of other Warli Adivasi families that weren't as fortunate as hers . Locals estimate that 70 Adivasi families lost their homes to the metro project. From 27, the number of padas is now down to 15. But the community is resilient. And this same quality has helped them become empowered entrepreneurs. While forest produce was once their means of sustenance, tree felling in 2019 made them realise they needed to divert their attention to other income streams. They needed to recalibrate their lives. Weaving a story of change For Geeta Page (32), hope equates to a sewing machine. Her mud home in Khambachapada has a single bulb, whose light doesn't reach her work spot. Despite the fact that it is 11 am when these interviews are being conducted, Geeta's home gives the semblance of late evening. Her eyes bear the brunt of her determination, as she sews in the dimness of the room. "We stitch when we get orders. It takes five days to make a quilt, and we get Rs 400 per quilt. A bag takes less time to stitch," she shares. Geeta, like many other women, isn't solely reliant on the factory job, which, she says, is subject to the whims of the bosses. She also gets orders from Cassandra Nazareth and her team, who have been working in the region since 2016, attempting to help the women of these communities in any way they can. Cassandra is joined by Mahesh Bariya, Blasia Pinto and Rita Newnes. Each of them was drawn to join the effort after they recognised what Cassandra was trying to do. Mahesh shares, "When we first entered these villages, we realised that the women were not allowed to go out of the house. They weren't working. So, we started skill development programmes in three villages in 2015 to sell the products made by the women: tote bags, drawstring pouches, laddoos , modaks ." The impact left an imprint on their psyche. "Then slowly, we started giving the women cloth on which they could paint Warli art, and these would be given outside for stitching into bags. That's when we came up with the idea that, instead of outsourcing the stitching, why don't we let the women themselves stitch and earn?" Mahesh adds. Of course, formalising the products for sale would require proper training. "So we gave them 27 machines. After the lockdown, they were approached by factories. It gives them a livelihood," he adds. Surekha, who has completed four years at the factory in Andheri's MIDC, says she likes the work. For many of the women, it was more a question of continuing what they knew. "I had learnt stitching in my mother's house before getting married," Surekha says. "It was nice to continue it through the job role." PF and medical cards Having a bank account and actually using it are two very different things. According to reports, in India, one in three bank accounts belongs to a woman, but women only hold about a fifth of the total money deposited in banks. Even when women possess banking skills, structural barriers leave them unable to utilise their deposits or access credit. But through this factory work, a different story is unfolding in Aarey Forest's hamlets. Take Renuka (28), for instance. "I stitch at the factory in MIDC. We also get medical cards. Every month, some amount (Rs 190) gets deducted from our salary, and we can avail of all facilities if required," she shares. Renuka's daughter and husband are also covered by the card. Prior to the factory job, she wasn't working. Now, Renuka feels empowered. Her story echoes many other women's too. For instance, Shubhangi Rohakar (35). Shubhangi looks forward to the Rs 15000 payment that lands in her account every month. She explains that, while her salary is Rs 20,000 at the factory, Rs 1800 goes towards the PF (Provident Fund, which is a retirement savings scheme), Rs 190 for the medical card and Rs 3000 for a loan that she has taken for the new home that they are building. "It's the first time in my life that I am getting a PF," she smiles. Shubhangi explains that they even got help from "Kashi ma'am (Cassandra, as the women call her) in opening their bank accounts, where they could deposit the money. "They helped in opening zero-balance bank accounts. A lot of women did not have accounts, and we did not know how to save our money. We had never stepped out of the village," she shares. The women are grateful that the stitching programme led to all of this. She's also found the ESIC Card (medical card) extremely useful. "Last year I had a stomach problem and needed a sonography and blood tests," she shares. Everything was done free of cost, as well as consultation with the doctor. The women are grateful that the stitching programme led to all of this. While many of their husbands were sceptical of this empowerment, Mahesh says once they started seeing the money come in, they were on board. Changing their lives through projects While sitting in Surekha's home, I spot a drum set. Her son Jatin (23) tells me it was given to him by Cassandra. Rita explains that this is part of the 'Aur Chalao' project, through which they give pre-loved (a better way of saying second-hand) items donated by Mumbaikars to families in Aarey. The drum set was one of these. But Jatin needed to go for classes to learn how to play the drums. And this is where his mother's additional income came in. "It also helped a lot in the home with rations and our college books," he says. This wasn't the first time Surekha was earning. As part of the tribal lunch programme started by Cassandra and her team, Surekha and the women would cook using forest produce and host lunches in the padas . Blasia says it would often make her nostalgic about vacations in Goa. "It was so nice to see these women cooking on firewood, with their children hanging around. As the husbands began to see that it was bringing in income, they started taking care of the children," she explains. The funds that they raised through the lunches were used to refurbish the existing borewells." Any additional income is welcome, says Arti Kirkire (31), who says that she is using her income from her factory job to make their home. "The sewing machines given to us helped us learn how to stitch," she shares. Arti's daughter was an infant when she first took up the factory job. Being away from 9.30 am to 6.30 pm was tough. "But the people in the community used to watch her; my in-laws too would help," she says. Getting a paycheque, she says, is a boon. "Have you bought anything for yourself?" I ask. "Just for the house," she smiles. Considering the shift ends in the evening, I wonder how the women travel and if it's safe. They share that a bus picks them up and drops them back. They are glad about this option as it's tough to predict the forest's rhythm. In 2022, 10 animal attacks were reported in Aarey in a single year. Geeta once used to fear venturing into the forest to relieve herself at night. She would control her urge. Now, the 47 bio-toilets (in close quarters to every home and shared among a couple of families each) are a blessing, she says. These have limited the human-animal conflict when community members would venture to attend nature's call. The Nazareth Foundation has also crowd-funded and got 12 domestic flour mills for the women, which eases their previous 2.5 km walk and helped with building water tanks with a capacity of 5000 litres. And while the world around them changes, their inner worlds change too, with a stitching programme helping them form their own identities. Sources 'In Photos | Warli Adivasis Recall Birsa Munda in Fight to Save Aarey' by Sushmita, Published on 11 November 2019. 'Aarey protests: Supreme Court steps in to save Mumbai trees after protests' , Published by the BBC on 7 November 2019. 'Aarey Adivasis: 'Then we lost this land of ours' by Aayna, Published on 24 October 2019. 'Financial Inclusion of Women: Current Evidence from India' by Sunaina Kumar, Published on 17 August 2023. '10 animal attacks reported from Aarey and SGNP in one year; residents fear for their lives' by Pratip Acharya, Published on 6 November 2022.

items.titleOriginal: Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk
items.description: Μια εκπληκτική νέα μελέτη δείχνει ότι ένα ισχυρότερο εμβόλιο γρίπης θα μπορούσε να προσφέρει στους ηλικιωμένους σημαντικά μεγαλύτερη προστασία έναντι της νόσου του Αλτσχάιμερ. Ερευνητές στο UTHealth Houston ανέλυσαν σχεδόν 200.000 ενήλικες ηλικίας 65 ετών και άνω και διαπίστωσαν ότι όσοι έλαβαν εμβόλιο υψηλής δόσης κατά της γρίπης είχαν σχεδόν 55% χαμηλότερο κίνδυνο να αναπτύξουν Αλτσχάιμερ.…
items.descriptionOriginal: A surprising new study suggests that a stronger flu shot could offer older adults significantly greater protection against Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UTHealth Houston analyzed nearly 200,000 adults ages 65 and older and found that those who received a high-dose influenza vaccine had a nearly 55% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's, compared with a 40% reduction previously associated with the standard-dose vaccine.

items.description: Η λέξη «ευεξία» μπορεί να δημιουργεί εικόνες από πολυτελείς περιποιήσεις σπα και πολυτελή καταφύγια, αλλά δεν χρειάζεται να κλείσετε μια πολυτελή απόδραση για να αυξήσετε τη ζωτικότητά σας – οι καθημερινές δραστηριότητες και οι μικρές, σκόπιμες συνήθειες μπορούν να είναι εξίσου αναζωογονητικές. Διαφορετικοί πολιτισμοί σε όλο τον κόσμο έχουν αναπτύξει εδώ και καιρό μοναδικές τεχνικές για την προώθηση της υγείας, της ευτυχίας και γενικότερα…
items.descriptionOriginal: The word “wellness” may conjure images of lavish spa treatments and high-end retreats, but you don’t have to book a luxury getaway to increase your vitality — everyday activities and small, intentional habits can be equally restorative. Different cultures around the world have long developed unique techniques to promote health, happiness, and overall well-being, from the Turkish concept of savoring idle pleasure to “forest bathing” in Japan. Join us as we explore 10 wellness traditions you can adopt to infuse more peace and balance into our often-overwhelming world. 1. Schemeren | The Netherlands antolikjan/iStock If you struggle to unwind after a long day, the Dutch concept of “dusking,” or “schemeren,” may be just what you’re looking for. The practice is remarkably effortless: Simply pull up a chair and pause for a while to watch the day turn into night. “Noticing twilight requires a persistent kind of attention. It’s like a shy, rare animal. You have to take your time. Stay focused,” author Marjolijn van Heemstra told the BBC , adding that it’s an important opportunity to reconnect with the world around us. “If you don’t know a tree, even if it’s in front of your house, because you never take the time to look at it, you don’t mind it being cut,” she said. “So, it’s about seeing things and trying to establish a relationship with them and then maybe caring for them.” 2. La Passeggiata | Italy Another evening ritual — la passeggiata — is a bit more active. In Italy, many people take an after-dinner stroll around town, which offers a way to connect with neighbors, reduce stress, and improve digestion, per the BBC . Although walking is widely recommended as an accessible and effective exercise , la passeggiata is more about relaxation and social bonds than fitness. 3. Hygge | Denmark Liudmila Chernetska/iStock Scandinavian winters tend to be long and dark, but the Danish tradition of hygge can make the season more enjoyable. Stemming from an Old Norse word meaning “protected from the outside world,” hygge centers on creating a cozy, comfortable environment, with an emphasis on self-care, relaxation, and spending time with loved ones. While it’s often associated with tangible things like warm drinks and soft blankets, it’s also a mindset focused on making small moments feel more meaningful. 4. Ubuntu | Southern Africa In certain sub-Saharan African cultures, including the Zulu and Xhosa, the philosophy and practice of ubuntu emphasize the importance of community and interconnectedness. Although it goes by many different names, ubuntu is apparent throughout societies across the continent, according to The Open University . At its core, it emphasizes the role individuals play in contributing to the greater good through intentional connection, mutual support, and a shared commitment to equality, equity, and fairness. In daily life, this can look like sharing resources and checking in on neighbors. As a whole, it’s about recognizing the humanity in everyone you meet. And the benefits may extend beyond your community: Research suggests that being kind to others can help your own well-being, too. 5. Sobremesa | Spain and Latin America JulieanneBirch/iStock Another custom grounded in community is “sobremesa,” which means “upon the table.” Popular in Spain and throughout Latin America, the centuries-old way of life involves lingering after a meal to relax, savor the moment, and chat — sometimes for hours. “It’s about an interchange of experiences, knowledge, and laughs. It encourages you to be present, not worrying about your troubles, and appreciate the simple moments in life,” Mexico City restaurateur Lorea Olavarri told Food & Wine . 6. Keyif | Turkey Turkey is famous for its hammam spas, but one of its perhaps lesser-known wellness traditions can be embraced anywhere. Keyif, “an ancient art of meaningful idleness,” is a state of mind focused on finding quiet joy in simple pleasures, per Eastern Turkey Tours . Unlike simply unwinding, keyif involves being fully present and savoring the more subdued moments, from sipping your first cup of coffee in the morning while watching the sun rise to gazing out the window and listening to the birds. 7. Dadirri | Australia Thurtell/iStock In Australia’s First Nations communities, the art of deep, intentional listening — often called dadirri — is an integral part of cultural preservation, community cohesion, and individual well-being. The ancient practice encourages people to connect with one another and the natural world, according to Aboriginal learning platform Creative Spirits . But it also extends beyond that to encompass self-reflection, contemplation, and an awareness of your origins, purpose, and place in the world. “It does wonders for a person to just be still and listen to someone else talk about their life and how they probably came through things,” late Aboriginal singer-songwriter Archie Roach once said about the importance of mindful listening, per the platform, adding: “You never know what you’ll learn.” 8. Shinrin-Yoku | Japan Ample research points to the mental and physical benefits of spending time in nature, and the Japanese tradition of shinrin-yoku, or forest bathing, can help you reap them. Despite the name, there are no bathtubs involved, and even the forest is optional. All it takes is spending some time in a green space and using your senses to take it all in, whether at a botanical garden, city park, or lush woodland. Touch the soft moss, breathe in the fresh air, and listen to the birds as you gaze at the trees. “Forest therapy [can help us] see the truth that we are interconnected and interdependent. It offers us intentional time to be with ourselves, each other, and the natural world,” Regan Stacey, founder of The Forest Therapy School , told Vogue . 9. Friluftsliv | Norway Glenn Pettersen/iStock Meaning “open-air living,” this philosophy focuses on connecting with nature year-round, regardless of the weather. Popularized in the 1850s by Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen, friluftsliv remains a cultural mainstay throughout Scandinavia, according to the BBC . In fact, many employers in the region build outdoor recreation time into the workday. Although a Monday morning hike may not be realistic for everyone, we can all embrace friluftsliv by setting aside time to venture outside as often as we can. 10. Rhythmic Movement and Dance | Various African Cultures While not a singular tradition, dance is central to numerous cultures across the African continent and its diasporas . Although often ritualistic or ceremonial, moving one’s body rhythmically to music is also an integral part of everyday life that can foster both community and individual well-being. “Dancing is a full-body workout that benefits both the mind and body,” Liza Osagie-Clouard, orthopedic surgeon and founder of Solice Health in London, England, told British Vogue . “It improves cardiovascular health, increases flexibility, strengthens muscles, and enhances coordination,” she added. Moreover, listening to music — including the rhythmic drumming that often accompanies traditional dances — can stimulate the release of chemicals like dopamine and serotonin in the brain, helping to alleviate anxiety, enhance mood, and facilitate emotional release. RELATED: A Connection to Nature Fuels Well‑Being Worldwide, According to a Study of 38,000 People

items.title: Μετά από μια αποτυχημένη καλλιέργεια, ο 57χρονος αγρότης καλλιέργησε φράουλες χωρίς χώμα και έκανε 44 Lakh Rs σε πωλήσεις
items.titleOriginal: After a Failed Crop, 57-YO Farmer Grew Strawberries Without Soil & Made Rs 44 Lakh in Sales
items.description: «Η καλλιέργεια σταματά εντελώς κατά τους καλοκαιρινούς και τους μουσώνες μήνες, επειδή η καλλιέργεια φράουλας σε ανοιχτό χωράφι δεν μπορεί να επιβιώσει αυτού του είδους τη ζέστη και τις βροχοπτώσεις». Για γενιές, αυτός ήταν ο κύκλος της καλλιέργειας φράουλας στο Mahabaleshwar. Όταν ο καιρός ζεστάνει και φτάνουν οι βροχές, η εποχή της φράουλας φτάνει στο τέλος της. Αλλά ο 57χρονος Ketan Sodha…
items.descriptionOriginal: "Cultivation stops completely through summer and monsoon months, because open-field strawberry growing cannot survive that kind of heat and rainfall." For generations, this has been the cycle of strawberry farming in Mahabaleshwar . When the weather turns warm, and the rains arrive, the strawberry season comes to an end. But 57-year-old Ketan Sodha, who had never farmed before 2016, wanted to see whether the season could last longer. A fourth-generation Mumbaikar from a business family with no farming background, Ketan completed his BCom from K C College under Mumbai University. He spent years connecting agricultural landowners with buyers across Maharashtra. Then, in 2016, demonetisation changed the business he knew. "What was available was Rs 25,000 an acre. In two years, it went up to Rs 3 lakh," he recalls of the agricultural land boom he had witnessed. But when demonetisation hit, that business slowed dramatically. "I had to start something new, so I decided to switch over to Mahabaleshwar for strawberries," he tells The Better India. Today, his venture, Berry Fresh Agrotech LLP, has a soilless polyhouse in Mahabaleshwar with the capacity to grow 19,500 strawberry plants. The farm has reportedly produced around 8,000 kg of fruit and generated Rs 44 lakh in sales. But getting here began with 5,000 plants, a failed crop, and a man from Mumbai learning to farm for the first time. How a first-time farmer learnt from his mistakes His work dealing in agricultural land took him across Maharashtra, usually within 200 km of Mumbai. One of the routes he travelled frequently was towards Goa, passing through Poladpur and the foothills of Mahabaleshwar. 57-year-old Ketan Sodha, who had never farmed before 2016, wanted to see whether the season could last longer. For someone used to Mumbai, Mahabaleshwar felt like another world. "I was born and raised in Mumbai, so coming here was a great delight for me. The city is hot, humid and congested, whereas spending a night in the cool hills around Poladpur felt like a completely different world," he admits. He first became interested in strawberries around 2012-13. After his land business slowed in 2016, he bought 5,000 plants from a local farmer and tried growing them himself. "The first year actually was a disaster," he says. But he did not walk away. In 2017, he increased the number of plants to 10,000. This time, the results were different. He began producing more fruit than many conventional growers around him who had been cultivating strawberries for decades. "My name began spreading in the area, and people started saying, 'This guy seems to know something we don't,'" he recalls. Some farmers began approaching him for partnerships, and he accepted a few of those opportunities. By 2019, he had entered into a partnership and started cultivating strawberries across nine acres. By the 2020-21 season, his operations had expanded to almost 40 acres across three sites. He was also working with imported planting material and developing his own nurseries. But even as his farming operations grew, the weather remained a challenge he could not control. The rain spoilt his hard work Mahabaleshwar may be known for its strawberries, but the crop is traditionally grown in open fields. That leaves the plants exposed to everything the weather brings. Ketan repeatedly saw the same problem during the years he spent growing the fruit conventionally. Unseasonal rain would arrive around November and early December, just when the crop was reaching its peak. The rain could set the crop back by 15 to 20 days. "You need to recover the crop, take care of it, spray some fungicides, because the unexpected rain creates a lot of nuisance," he says. There was another limitation too. Once summer and the monsoon arrived, conventional strawberry cultivation stopped. He began wondering whether changing the environment in which strawberries grew could help him extend the season, rather than leaving his harvest at the mercy of the weather. 4 countries, countless lessons and one Indian challenge In 2021-22, he travelled to Italy, Spain, Egypt and Turkey. He met nursery owners and hydroponic growers and spoke to consultants from several countries, including Israel, the UK, New Zealand, Australia and the US. He came back with plenty of information. But he also came back with an important realisation. A system that worked perfectly in another country could not blindly be copied in India. "My country's challenges are very different from what they are working on in their own native area," he says. He began developing a model suited to the conditions in Mahabaleshwar. Berry Fresh Agrotech LLP was incorporated on 14 October 2022. He had already been cultivating strawberries conventionally with local farmers. But the company's soilless plantation began in November 2024. Before the first plants went into the new system, he spent around three-and-a-half months searching for suitable land , despite having worked in the region for years. He eventually leased two acres. On this land, he built a 1,500-square-metre polyhouse designed to accommodate 19,500 strawberry plants. And this time, there would be no soil. A strawberry farm without soil Inside his polyhouse, the plants grow in cocopeat, a growing medium made from coconut husk. Traditional strawberry fields use the same soil year after year, increasing the risk of soil-borne diseases. Growing the plants in cocopeat helps reduce this risk. The plants are grown under a retractable roof in an openable polyhouse. A misting system helps manage the growing environment. The farm is also located at an altitude of around 1,400 metres. Even when temperatures rise suddenly in the plains, Mahabaleshwar's elevation gives the plants a natural advantage. Then comes water. Through an automated fertigation system, which delivers water and nutrients together, each plant receives approximately 75 ml of nutrient solution over 24 hours. His farm also harvests rainwater and stores it for use. Before entering the growing system, the water is treated with ozone. Today, his venture, Berry Fresh Agrotech LLP, has a soilless polyhouse in Mahabaleshwar with the capacity to grow 19,500 strawberry plants. This allows him to manage the water supply while reducing dependence on external sources or groundwater. "The plant is never stressed by too much or too little water," he explains. Together, the soilless growing medium, measured nutrients, protected environment and milder temperatures help Ketan keep his strawberry plants growing during periods when conventional cultivation stops. "The real innovation here is not one single trick, but removing every variable, one by one, that used to force conventional growers to stop," he explains. There are parts of the process he does not disclose. Those, he says, are the lessons he has gathered through years of experimentation and practical work. And much of that learning came from problems he had to solve himself. When everything had to be rebuilt He had initially expected specialised vendors to provide much of the technology required for the farm. Instead, several systems needed to be fixed and recalibrated. The polyhouse took more than six months to complete. The automation and irrigation systems also required considerable attention. Even finding suitable hydroponic-grade fertilisers proved difficult. Eventually, he and his team began inspecting, repairing and adjusting the pipes, valves, sensors, controllers and irrigation lines themselves. "We started this journey to grow strawberries, not to become experts in polyhouse construction, irrigation, automation and fertigation," he says. "When a problem arises, we don't have to wait for someone to fly in or send a technician," he says. "We understand our systems because we have rebuilt many of them ourselves." The entire setup required an investment in the seven-figure range, although he does not want to disclose the exact amount. He viewed the first facility as a place to experiment and learn, rather than recover the investment immediately. Testing 19 varieties for Indian conditions Ketan is among only around 12 to 15 growers in India involved in importing strawberry planting material. Berry Fresh is currently conducting trials involving 19 strawberry varieties from countries including Florida, Spain, Italy, Uruguay and Japan. This season, the farm has also added a variety from the Netherlands. Different varieties respond differently to climate and disease, and can vary in yield, taste and fruit quality. A variety that performs well abroad may struggle in Indian conditions. Through these trials, Ketan wants to identify which varieties grow best here and eventually make better planting material accessible to other farmers. He is also exploring the possibility of securing exclusive rights to some foreign genetics for India as he works towards expanding the business. The plants are grown under a retractable roof in an openable polyhouse. From a failed crop to Rs 44 lakh in sales The current facility has an installed capacity of 19,500 plants and operates at around 90 percent capacity. For the period from January 2024 to December 2025, Ketan reports an average harvest of 408 grams per plant, with production of approximately 3.2 kg per square metre. Across the production figures shared by Berry Fresh, the venture has reportedly harvested approximately 8,000 kg of strawberries and generated around Rs 44 lakh in revenue through business-to-business (B2B) and direct-to-consumer (B2C) sales. The strawberries are sold at an approximate price of Rs 400 to Rs 600 per kg, depending on the customer and order. Around 60 percent of sales are B2C, while 40 percent are B2B. Its customers are spread across Mumbai, Mahabaleshwar, Delhi, Bhopal, Ahmedabad, Indore, Udupi and Goa. There is no comprehensive digital marketing operation behind those sales. Ketan admits he has no social media presence. Instead, his customers have largely found him through word of mouth. And many of them have stayed. 'Do not pay if you do not like it' Prashant Tatia (54), from Bhopal, runs a premium fruit and dry-fruit shop. He has known Ketan since 2021 and started purchasing strawberries from Berry Fresh in January 2025. Berry Fresh Agrotech LLP was incorporated on 14 October 2022. "The strawberries produced by the farm are distinctly different from conventionally grown open-field varieties," says Prashant. "They stand out for their vibrant colour, natural shine, uniform shape, exceptional taste, higher sweetness, longer shelf life, and outstandingly rich aroma." For Prashant, the consistency matters just as much as the taste. He says the quality remains consistent even during the off-season. "What sets Berry Fresh apart is its year-round availability and consistently high quality," he says. Luvjeet Singh, an imported fruit dealer from Vashi, Mumbai, began purchasing from the venture in November 2025. Ketan had contacted him the previous month. "He simply quoted, 'Do not pay if you do not like it,'" Luvjeet recalls. "I was surprised by his confidence, hence thought of trying. It was worth his claim." He says the berries differ in their colour, shine, shape, sweetness, aroma and shelf life, and believes his customers are willing to pay for better-quality produce. In Ahmedabad, 25-year-old Apurva Shelat came across the business through a common friend. She began buying the strawberries in November 2025. "After talking to the founder, I developed trust, so I decided to try his strawberries," she says. "I found that the quality was much better, and my community also liked them very much." She has also visited the farm. For someone who had never seen this kind of strawberry cultivation before, the experience changed the way she looked at farming. "I was impressed by how clean, well-organised and professionally managed the farm was. Seeing the hydroponic system for the first time also changed my understanding of modern farming," she says. His next bet: 2 lakh plants across 5 acres For now, Berry Fresh operates only in Mahabaleshwar. But the founder is already thinking beyond the 19,500 plants. He is currently at the investor-discussion stage for a proposed five-acre facility with a minimum capacity of around 200,000 plants. He wants to build the next farm using everything he has learnt from the first, with the hope of eventually replicating the model in other parts of India where the climate is suitable. The opportunity, in his view, is to grow strawberries during months when fewer farmers can supply them, and when the fruit can fetch better prices. "If we can extend the production window at both ends, early fruit before the regular season starts, and no-season fruit after everyone else has stopped, both of those windows fetch the highest value in the market," he says. It is a different life from the one he knew in Mumbai. Ketan had no family farming background, and his first attempt at growing strawberries failed. Today, he spends his days learning how to help thousands of plants thrive in the hills he has come to love. On this land, he built a 1,500-square-metre polyhouse designed to accommodate 19,500 strawberry plants. "Every morning, birds wake me up before any alarm does," he says. "The air here is crisp, the spring water is clean, and there is a kind of peace around this farm that you cannot buy in Mumbai." For Ketan, the next challenge is taking what he has learnt from this first polyhouse to a much larger farm, while continuing to explore how far Mahabaleshwar's strawberry season can stretch. All pictures courtesy Ketan Sodha.

items.title: Τι θα γινόταν αν ένα Firecracker αφήσει χωρίς καπνό; Αυτός ο επιστήμονας του IISER βρήκε έναν ασυνήθιστο τρόπο να το φτιάξει
items.titleOriginal: What If a Firecracker Left No Smoke? This IISER Scientist Found an Unusual Way to Make One
items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία είναι μέρος του "India Invented This?" — Η εβδομαδιαία σειρά trivia του The Better India που αποκαλύπτει τα μυαλά, τις ιδέες και τις καινοτομίες των Ινδών πίσω από εφευρέσεις που έχουν διαμορφώσει τον τρόπο που ζούμε. Από έξυπνες λύσεις που δημιουργήθηκαν από επιστήμονες και μηχανικούς έως τεχνολογίες που αναπτύχθηκαν ως απάντηση σε μερικές από τις μεγαλύτερες προκλήσεις της Ινδίας, κάθε ιστορία πάει μακρυά…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of "India Invented This?" — The Better India's weekly trivia series that uncovers the Indian minds, ideas and innovations behind inventions that have shaped the way we live. From ingenious solutions created by scientists and engineers to technologies developed in response to some of India's biggest challenges, each story goes beyond the invention to explore the problem it solved, the impact it created and why it still matters today. There is something special about the moment a child lights their first sparkler. The excitement of holding it, the little circles they draw in the air, and the delight of watching it fade into tiny glowing embers are memories that often stay with us long after childhood. For generations, firecrackers have been part of how many Indian families celebrate Diwali. But what if the thrill of watching something burst into the sky did not have to come with clouds of smoke, lingering gunpowder smells and piles of burnt debris? That was the question Dr Samrat Ghosh, a chemical scientist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER), Mohali, decided to explore. His answer? A firecracker that uses an entirely different approach to create the familiar excitement of fireworks, without the smoke and particulate emissions associated with conventional crackers. And the interesting part is that his innovation began with something most people would simply throw away: an empty plastic bottle. From waste bottles to a new kind of firecracker In October 2017, following concerns about firecracker pollution and a Supreme Court order temporarily restricting their use in the NCR, then Union Environment Minister Dr Harsh Vardhan called upon scientists to develop safer alternatives , including electronic firecrackers. Dr Samrat took up the challenge. A discarded plastic bottle became the starting point for an innovation that rethinks conventional fireworks. Photograph: ( The Indian Express ) An assistant professor in IISER Mohali's Department of Chemical Sciences, he drew upon his expertise in combustion chemistry to develop what became known as the IISER-M pollution-free firecracker. The first prototype was built using recycled plastic bottles and a specially developed combustible formulation. Instead of the conventional arrangement of chemicals packed into a paper casing, his device worked through a small launcher mechanism. Here's how it worked: When triggered by a spark , the combustible material ignited and generated pressure, pushing the bottle upwards like a rocket. The launch produced a loud bang, recreating some of the excitement associated with traditional fireworks. But the real innovation lay in what happened around it. No smoke, no leftover debris, and even a fragrance! Unlike conventional firecrackers, Ghosh's formulation was designed to produce no visible smoke or particulate matter. The device also left no conventional firecracker debris behind. Another unusual feature was that the sound level could be adjusted, allowing users to customise how loud the explosion was. Depending on the ingredients used in the combustible formulation , the device could even release a fragrance into the air. The idea was to replace the familiar smell of gunpowder with something more pleasant. Imagine finishing Diwali celebrations with the scent of lavender rather than burnt chemicals! The IISER-M firecracker uses a launcher mechanism to recreate the excitement of traditional rockets. Photograph: ( ANI News ) His team developed both aerial and non-aerial prototypes. The device was also designed to be reusable, with the bottle being launched rather than destroyed in the process. The next experiment involved something unexpected A year after developing the prototype, Ghosh and his team began exploring ways to make the formulation more affordable. Their next experiment involved distilled cow urine. In 2019, the team had developed a cheaper version of its green firecracker using this ingredient. According to Ghosh, incorporating distilled cow urine reduced the cost of the formulation by 50%, without changing its performance in terms of sound, light and flight. The team also maintained that its organic formulation produced no particulate-matter emissions. An emission study was being conducted at IISER to analyse the gases released during combustion. The experiment was also driven by a practical consideration: making the technology affordable enough to explore wider adoption. A different way to look at celebration For Ghosh, the idea was never simply to make another firecracker. It was to rethink how fireworks could work while addressing some of the problems associated with conventional ones. His innovation also had potential applications beyond Diwali. The device could potentially be used to drive animals away from agricultural fields or help clear airport runways. The technology was still under development according to the reports in 2018, and its commercialisation and wider adoption were not established. The innovation was still awaiting patents at the time of the reports, and its journey towards wider commercial use remained a work in progress. The innovation explores alternatives to conventional crackers, including adjustable sound levels and fragrance-releasing formulations. Photograph: ( Hindustan Times ) But perhaps that is what makes the experiment interesting. It shows how even the most familiar traditions can leave room for new ideas. A discarded plastic bottle, a scientist's curiosity and a desire to reduce pollution came together to challenge the way we think about firecrackers. And who knows? With further research and development, innovations like Ghosh's could one day help make the excitement of Diwali a little kinder to the air we all share. Είναι μια ειλικρινής περιγραφή του πώς η πείνα για μεταμόρφωση μπορεί να γίνει η δική της παγίδα και η ήπια διαδικασία συντονισμού με κάθε στιγμή. Η στροφή ήρθε αθόρυβα, μέσα από ένα μόνο χτύπημα…
items.descriptionOriginal: A Polish monk began each day with seven bows -- a gesture of apology toward a father he couldn't face. Bhikshu Jin Wei's story is not a tidy arc of spiritual progress; it's an honest account of how the hunger for transformation can become its own trap, and the gentle process of attuning to each moment. The turning came quietly, through a single word: a Thai Forest monk suggested a one-word loving-kindness mantra, and Jin Wei sat in the meditation hall asking himself what his word was. Immediately, it came: "safe". What followed was the discovery that the compassion he had been excavating through discipline had been waiting in his body all along -- "our body remembers our trauma," he reflects, "but the body also keeps the love." While on a trip back to Poland earlier this year, he experienced profound, full-circle moments along a softening journey: giving a talk at his own university and sitting down to a vegetarian lunch lovingly offered by his meat-eating family. The monastery, he suggests, is not only a physical place but a quality of listening, available to anyone willing to stop and ask what word is waiting to open their heart.

items.descriptionOriginal: The first sign that winter has arrived in many North Indian kitchens is not the chill in the morning air, but the sight of a heap of red carrots at the vegetable market. For a few months, the deep-red carrot takes centre stage in markets across Delhi and other parts of North India, where shoppers who buy orange carrots through much of the year will seek out this seasonal variety. But the red carrot's place in the winter kitchen is tied to more than nostalgia. Its cultivation depends on growing conditions, including temperature, raising questions about what warmer winters could mean for a crop so closely associated with the season. Why red carrots rule the winter kitchen Red carrots, commonly known as lal gajar, are prized for their deep colour, sweetness and juiciness. Their arrival makes a difference to dishes in which the vegetable is the main ingredient, rather than simply one component of a meal. In gajar ka halwa, grated red carrots cook down with milk and ghee to produce the dessert's characteristic colour and flavour. Kanji draws on a different tradition: carrot sticks ferment in water seasoned with mustard seeds, salt and spices, producing a sharp, tangy drink. Red carrots are also used in winter salads, cooked vegetable dishes and pickles. Its arrival signals the season for halwa made in large batches, jars of kanji left to ferment and pickles prepared for later consumption. Photograph: (Bliss of Cooking; Your Everyday Cook) The seasonal preference for red carrots is therefore not simply a switch from one colour to another. It is also about the taste, texture and culinary traditions associated with the red variety. There is a scientific reason to look beyond colour. In a study published in 2016 in the Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences, researchers Swati Saha, Pritam Kalia, Amish Kumar Sureja and S Sarkar at the ICAR–Indian Agricultural Research Institute in New Delhi examined 38 tropical carrot lines over four consecutive years, from 2009 to 2012. They compared characteristics including root weight, colour and nutritional composition. The researchers found considerable differences in the amount of carotenoids and other pigments present in the carrots. One red line, IPC-11 red, contained 9.99 milligrams of total carotenoids per 100 grams. The study also found that some carrot lines performed well under high-temperature conditions , making them potential candidates for future breeding. A crop shaped by temperature Carrots are generally associated with cool-season cultivation, although tropical varieties have been developed to grow under warmer conditions. Temperature influences root development, yield and quality, making it an important factor in determining how successfully a variety performs. Saha and her colleagues put it simply: 'Temperature influences growth, yield and quality of carrots in many different ways.' Their research was not a study of climate change in farmers' fields. Instead, it explored whether particular carrot lines could withstand heat while retaining desirable characteristics. The researchers noted that 'some inbreds performed well under extreme high temperature without affecting any quality attributes'. Such lines, they suggested, could be selected for further breeding. Temperature influences root development, yield and quality, making it an important factor in determining how successfully a variety performs. Photograph: (Adobe Stock) India's agricultural research system also maintains red varieties suited to local growing conditions. In a 2020 article in the ICAR journal Indian Horticulture, researchers described Pusa Kesar as a variety with deep-red roots and a small, deep-red core. They also documented Pusa Rudhira, developed by ICAR-IARI in New Delhi, as a tropical variety with dark-red roots that matures around 85–90 days after sowing and is suitable for cultivation in the National Capital Region. These varieties show how researchers have worked to develop carrots suited to India's agricultural conditions. But they also raise a question: how might the conditions in which red carrots are grown change as temperatures rise? What warming winters could mean The 2016 study offers a useful starting point for understanding the risks. In discussing earlier research on carrot cultivation, Saha and her colleagues noted that temperatures above 25 C could result in unmarketable roots and lower yields. They also cited research indicating that temperatures below 10 C or above 30 C could produce lighter-coloured roots. These findings point to a potential concern for growers: that heat can affect not just how much a crop produces, but also the appearance and quality of its roots. For red carrots, whose colour is central to their appeal, that factor is important. However, these temperature findings should not be treated as proof that climate change is already reducing red carrot production in North India. The effects depend on the variety, the timing of sowing, soil conditions, irrigation and temperatures at different stages of growth. Preserving a seasonal flavour The red carrot's winter popularity connects agriculture to everyday food traditions. Its arrival signals the season for halwa made in large batches, jars of kanji left to ferment and pickles prepared for later consumption. The future of this seasonal crop will depend partly on how effectively farmers and breeders respond to changing growing conditions. Until then, the seasonal rush for red carrots remains both a culinary tradition and a reason to pay closer attention to the crops that connect India's winter kitchens to its changing climate. Sources: 'Climate change and vegetable crops cultivation: A review' : By The Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences, Published on 27 April 2018 'Response of carrot (Daucus carota L.) cultivars to different sowing dates on growth and yield' : By P Madhavi Latha, P Syam Sundar Reddy, Ramanjaneya Reddy, V Sudha Vani, Published on 30 December 2015 'Breeding tropical carrots (Daucus carota) for enhanced nutrition and high temperature stress' : By ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute, Pusa, Published on 11 July 2016

items.title: «Είχαν χάσει την ελπίδα τους»: Πώς μια ομάδα που υποστηρίζεται από IIT πήρε τρόφιμα και φάρμακα σε 1000+ άτομα στο Πλημμυρισμένο Assam
items.titleOriginal: ‘They Had Lost Hope’: How an IIT-Backed Team Took Food & Meds to 1000+ People in Flood-Hit Assam
items.description: «Άνθρωποι, ζώα, γεωργικά χωράφια – τα πάντα έχουν πληγεί σοβαρά», λέει ο Dakshina, κάτοικος της Nazira στο Assam που είδε τις πλημμύρες. «Δεν υπήρχαν δρόμοι, ούτε γέφυρες, ούτε προσβάσιμες διαδρομές γιατί τα πάντα ήταν βυθισμένα στο νερό». Όταν τα νερά της πλημμύρας καταπίνουν δρόμους, καλύπτουν γέφυρες και περιβάλλουν ολόκληρους οικισμούς, ζητώντας βοήθεια στο p…
items.descriptionOriginal: "People, animals, agricultural fields – everything has been severely affected," says Dakshina, a resident of Nazira in Assam who witnessed the floods. "There were no roads, no bridges, and no accessible routes because everything was submerged in water." When floodwaters swallow roads, cover bridges and surround entire settlements, getting help to people becomes a race against time. In Assam, where communities face recurring floods, even getting essential supplies to stranded residents can become a challenge. During the recent floods in Upper Assam, parts of Sivasagar and other affected districts faced precisely this problem. Water had cut off communities from the road network, and in some places, even boats struggled to reach people because the water was too shallow. For residents, the uncertainty was frightening. People had to find safer ground while trying to save their livestock and livelihoods. Some were stranded in places where rescue teams could not easily reach them. In this situation, Drones Tech Lab, a deep-tech company incubated at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Guwahati, deployed payload-carrying drones to deliver food, water, medicines and other essentials across three districts in Assam. The operation reached more than 1,000 people in locations where even conventional relief efforts faced access constraints. The drones also helped survey affected areas and identify stranded residents, giving relief and rescue teams a clearer picture of where assistance was needed. For Dakshina, the intervention revealed a side of drone technology she had never seen before. When floodwaters cut off roads and bridges, drones helped deliver essential supplies to communities stranded in Assam. "Usually, we know drones as something used for taking videos at parties, weddings, or similar events," she says. "But this time, we saw for the first time how drones can actually help people during a disaster." Behind this intervention was technology that had taken years to develop , test and adapt for India's challenging terrain. 'We wanted India to build its own drones' Founded in 2016 by Ritesh Kanu, Biswajit Dey and Debajit Deka, Drones Tech Lab began with a vision to develop indigenous drone capabilities in a country that relied heavily on foreign technology. At the time, India's drone ecosystem was still taking shape. Awareness of its applications beyond photography was limited, access to funding was difficult, and building hardware-intensive technology came with significant challenges. Kanu says the founders wanted to address the dependence on imported systems and build technology suited to India's operational needs. "India has been a consumer of drone technology right from the start," he says. "We had a belief and a vision that we should be building in assets." For the team, indigenous technology did not mean manufacturing every component locally from day one. It meant developing intellectual property, designing system architecture, integrating software and engineering drones for specific missions. Their early work was influenced by the challenges faced by defence personnel operating in difficult environments. The founders saw how technology could help reduce risks to human life, particularly when information about a location or threat was difficult to obtain. Through its association with IIT Guwahati, the company developed unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), flight systems, software and specialised payload mechanisms. Developed at IIT Guwahati, Drones Tech Lab's heavy-payload drone can carry up to 30 kg, with applications ranging from disaster response to healthcare logistics. One of its developments was a heavy-payload drone with an indigenous carbon-fibre frame capable of carrying up to 30 kg. The company has since worked across disaster response, defence, healthcare logistics, mapping, conservation and infrastructure. Kanu compares a drone's carbon-fibre frame to a car's chassis: it holds the different components together. Its propulsion system, which includes motors and electronic speed controllers, provides the force needed to lift and move the drone. The real capability, however, lies in how these components work together. By modifying software, propulsion systems and payload-release mechanisms, the team can adapt a drone to the requirements of a particular mission. During a flood , that could mean carrying essential supplies to a settlement cut off by water. A drone can take help to floot-hit villages The first challenge during a flood is understanding what is happening on the ground. Which settlements are cut off? Where are people stranded? Which areas need supplies most urgently? And how can rescue teams approach them safely? Drones can survey affected areas from above, helping teams map isolated pockets and prioritise their response. Once a delivery point is identified, its coordinates can be entered into the flight plan. The drone then carries the supplies to the designated location, where the package is released for people on the ground to collect. During the Assam operation , Drones Tech Lab used drones with a payload capacity of around 5 kg per flight. They travelled approximately 5 km on missions that took about 25 minutes. The smaller payload was a deliberate choice based on the conditions. "We have drones that can carry more than 50 kilos also," says Kanu. "But the situation demanded a drone with a payload capacity of around 5 kg to make the operation more effective." The process involved much more than flying an aircraft. The team mapped affected locations, coordinated with government officials, prepared supply packets and identified suitable delivery points. Local authorities helped the team reach launch locations and coordinate its work with relief efforts. During the Assam floods, the team used drones carrying around 5 kg per flight, covering approximately 5 km in 25 minutes. Together, these steps helped the team plan where supplies needed to go and how to get them there. Drones also helped responders understand the condition of stranded residents. Dakshina recalls how aerial surveys identified people on rooftops or trapped alongside their livestock, while providing information about water levels and possible routes for rescue teams. When immediate physical rescue was not possible, aerial assessments helped teams determine whether people had food and water and needed urgent assistance. Every disaster taught them something new The company had already deployed its technology during the 2022 Assam floods and following Cyclone Amphan in West Bengal's Sundarbans. Each operation offered lessons in mapping affected areas, locating stranded communities and improving the software used to plan missions. "It's not just a camera drone being flown and then dropping food material somewhere," says Kanu. "The most important thing is that it has to be effective, and that comes only when you have the data." The drones also conducted aerial surveys, helping rescue teams identify people stranded on rooftops and locate areas requiring urgent assistance. He explains that repeated field deployments have helped the team improve how it analyses affected areas and identifies locations that should be prioritised. The goal is to reduce the time between identifying a need and delivering assistance. The company's work extends beyond floods , too. Drones Tech Lab has worked with the Kolkata Municipal Corporation on dengue-control and medicine-spraying operations, supported aerial monitoring and surveillance at Kaziranga National Park, and undertaken healthcare logistics work with AIIMS using payload drones. Each of these applications requires the team to adapt its software, equipment and flight operations to the work being done on the ground. How can drones reach people faster next time? The work also draws on the ecosystem around IIT Guwahati, where Professor Parameshwar K. Iyer is associated with the Centre for Drone Technology. Iyer says efforts to strengthen the region's drone ecosystem gained momentum during the pandemic, when disaster management discussions highlighted the need for interdisciplinary solutions. Facilities for testing drones and training pilots became an important part of that effort. IIT Guwahati established designated areas for drone testing and operations, helping create infrastructure for companies and researchers working in the Northeast. The importance of having this infrastructure in place became clear during the recent Assam floods, when the response had to move quickly. After discussions with the team and state authorities, the drones and personnel were sent to Sivasagar overnight. Within 24 hours, the team was on the ground, surveying affected areas and helping identify stranded residents. For Iyer, the larger question is how such capabilities can be made available before the next emergency. "We have to be ready for any kind of disaster," he says. For communities cut off by floodwaters, drones offered a way to receive essential supplies and help rescue teams locate people waiting for assistance. Photograph: ( Hindustan Times ) He believes establishing drone facilities and services at multiple locations across vulnerable regions could reduce response times and help assistance reach communities faster. Such preparedness would require coordination between technology providers, local administrations and disaster-management agencies. Drones cannot replace evacuation teams, medical care or the wider relief network communities depend on. They can, however, help responders understand what is happening in areas that are difficult to reach and deliver limited supplies while further assistance is organised. 'They had lost hope of receiving relief' For Kanu, the impact of the Assam deployment was best understood through the reactions of people receiving help, rather than the distances flown or the weight carried by the drones. He remembers how some residents had lost hope of receiving relief because no one could easily reach them. Seeing supplies arrive by drone was an unfamiliar experience. "They had actually lost hope of receiving relief because they had no access to it," he says. "When we look back at the work we have put into building this company over the past 10 years, moments like these show us why we started. We may be sitting in Calcutta, working on technology day and night, but seeing it reach people who need help makes that journey worthwhile." As disasters continue to test communities and emergency services, drones offer one way to bridge the gap between those who need help and those trying to reach them. How effectively they can do this depends on their ability to work alongside relief teams on the ground. In Assam, technology developed over nearly a decade found an urgent purpose: carrying essential supplies across flooded terrain to people waiting for help. The next step is ensuring that when roads disappear again, the teams, infrastructure and coordination needed to respond are already in place. The team's efforts brought essential supplies and hope to communities cut off by the floods. For Dakshina, the experience is reason enough to make the technology available in more places. She hopes drones can help locate people and animals in danger and direct assistance towards areas that remain difficult to access. "I sincerely hope that such systems and technologies will be made available in more places," she says. All images courtesy Drones Tech Lab team

items.descriptionOriginal: Visitors to London’s British Museum can admire a remarkable example of Roman ingenuity that’s considered one of the seven glass wonders of the world. Dated to the fourth century, the ornate Lycurgus Cup is a soft jade green — or a striking ruby red, depending on where the light source is positioned. The goblet’s color-changing capability has long perplexed scientists. No one is sure exactly how it was created, but the consensus is that Romans added tiny bits of gold and silver to their glass mixture, forming layers of nanoparticles that interact with light differently depending on their size and shape. Experts had struggled to devise a reliable method of re-creating the material in quantity, but now, for the first time, the mystery appears to have been solved. Melding an ancient recipe with modern science, a glass specialist from the University of Sheffield has reproduced the effect, and commissioned a sculpture that pays homage to the original. Lisa Hollands, with the institution’s School of Chemical, Materials, and Biological Engineering, took on the challenge, which was “very much a labor of love,” per a news release from the university. She worked with a Roman glass expert to develop a base that mimicked those used nearly two millennia ago, then set about experimenting with different furnace types, oxygen levels, and more. She said she knew it would be a much more complicated task than simply sprinkling some gold and silver nanoparticles into a mixture, but did think at one point, “If the Romans could have seen me experimenting, they’d probably laugh and ask: ‘Why does she not know how to make this?’” Finally, Hollands landed on a recipe for glass that looked opaque green under reflected light but red when a light was shone directly on it. “To me, it’s magic,” she told The Guardian . So how exactly does it work? “White light is made up of many different colors and you see this when there is a rainbow in the sky. Nanoparticles are much smaller than the wavelengths of light and in certain conditions they block certain colors due to the light affecting the electrons in the atoms,” she explained to the outlet. “So, for this glass, if light is shone through it, the gold and silver particles block blue and green light, only allowing reds and oranges to pass through. If light is reflected off the surface, the particles have the effect of scattering the light, giving the opaque green color we see,” she continued. Hollands and her project manager approached U.K. glass artist Elliot Walker, who won Season 2 of Netflix’s Blown Away , to create a finished piece that could be exhibited at Sheffield’s upcoming Festival of the Mind, which runs Nov. 6-15. It will then go on permanent display at the university’s Turner Museum of Glass . “You can really get an idea of how the glass makers of the past would have adapted to this sort of glass; it’s like shaking their hands,” Walker said in the release. The Lycurgus Cup depicts the legend of King Lycurgus from Homer’s Iliad , showing the triumph of the Greek god Dionysus over the lawgiver Lycurgus . The 2026 homage bridges the time between the Roman artwork and now. “I wanted to keep the sculpture quite classical in form and to carry through the original story of Lycurgus shown on the cup, but we needed a blown element within this to really show the dichroic glass ,” said Walker. “The piece is a blend of the Lycurgus story and the Farnese Atlas sculpture , with the globe replaced by a cup.” RELATED: Researchers Re-Create 5,000-Year-Old Egyptian Blue, the World’s Oldest Synthetic Pigment Once Lost to Science
